We must absolutely preserve the guardrails that steward Americans’ privacy, and Congress accomplished much of that with RISA. But the hard truth is that Section 702 is one of the most valuable tools that we have to keep our people and our servicemembers safe. Allowing that tool to expire would jeopardize Americans in a dangerously irresponsible way — and we, as Congress, have a duty to prevent that. 

I urge my colleagues to listen to President Trump and reauthorize Section 702.

In the past, there have been compliance issues – including other surveillance programs being used against President Trump – but Congress made more than 50 reforms to FISA in 2024. It is a fundamentally different tool than it was before. 

And the surest indicator that things have changed is that President Trump, who was unlawfully and unjustly surveilled himself, has called on Congress to pass a clean reauthorization of Section 702.

What they don’t need is a warrant just to query the database itself.

Some argue they should. The concern is understandable, but it’s not how law enforcement typically works. When agencies lawfully collect intelligence, they’re allowed to analyze it. Requiring a warrant just to review already-collected intelligence would be like telling the DEA that they need a warrant every time they wanted to listen to a wiretap recording of a drug lord that they were already authorized to obtain.

Now the warrant issue: if the FBI comes across these lawfully collected communications and believes there’s a credible national security concern involving a U.S. person, they can review that information. But if they want to take further investigative steps, like conducting new surveillance or building a prosecutable criminal case, they have to go to a judge and get a warrant.

U.S. persons CANNOT be targeted under Section 702. And in fact, even when a targeted foreigner sets foot on US soil, their communications can no longer be monitored unless we get a warrant. That’s right: even foreign terrorists get those 4th amendment protections just because they set foot in the US. If a foreign terrorist overseas is emailing or texting someone in the United States, that communication of course is collected. Not because we “target” Americans, but because someone or some place i

Some members of our conference have privacy concerns. Philosophically, they’re not wrong to worry. I can see how the idea that the intelligence community could access Americans’ communications could be intimidating. But their opposition is rooted in a fundamental misunderstanding of how the program actually works.

Nobody seems to understand exactly what Section 702 is. To be completely clear – Section 702 targets foreign adversaries overseas. It’s a program that our military and intelligence communities have shown over and over again saves American lives.
